title: Pawn cover: what a pawn push in front of your king gives away
outcomes: Names the pawns that form the cover in front of a castled king
Names the holes that a pawn push in front of the king creates
Tells a push that creates holes (g6) from one that creates none (h6) and from one on the other wing
Names the enemy pieces that can move to a new hole next move

steps.text: A castled king hides behind his **pawn cover**: the pawns on his file and the files beside it, on the two ranks in front of him. A pawn guards the squares diagonally ahead of it, and when it steps forward it stops guarding them. A **hole** is a square on your third to fifth rank that none of your pawns attacks now or can attack later. An enemy piece can sit on a hole and no pawn can chase it away.

steps.caption: Black to move. His king stands on g8 behind the pawns f7, g7 and h7.

line.say: The g-pawn steps to g6. It no longer guards f6 or h6, and no other pawn can.
The white queen lands on h6. No black pawn attacks that square, now or later.

claims.statement: Before the move the holes in Black's camp are a4, a5, b6, c5, c6, d6.
After g6 the holes in Black's camp are a4, a5, b6, c5, c6, d6, f6, h6.
After g6 the queen on e3 attacks h6.
No black pawn attacks h6 once the queen is there.

steps.text: A hole matters when an enemy piece can reach it and your own pieces cannot cover it, so a push is a warning sign, a **rule of thumb**, not a ban. Some pushes create no hole at all, and a push on the other wing leaves the king's cover alone. Before a pawn move near your king, name the squares it stops guarding and the enemy pieces that could land there.

steps.title: One position, three pawn moves
steps.prompt: For each move, predict: does it give White a new hole on the f-, g- or h-file? Then check.
Which part is harder for you: seeing which squares a pawn stops guarding, or seeing which enemy piece can reach them? Name one pawn move near the king from your own games and check it on the board.
